title: Arrest at Lahore
hookLine: summoned by the emperor Jahangir's order, Guru Arjan is imprisoned and tortured in the heat of Lahore

cards: Come to Lahore. In 1605 a new emperor, Jahangir, takes the Mughal throne, and within a year his order reaches Guru Arjan. It is early summer on the plains of Punjab, the hottest time of the year.
Look at the week behind him: a quiet youngest son chosen as Guru, letters of longing from Lahore, a jealous brother, a house with four doors, a book gathered from many voices and given a home.
The Guru has built a great deal in a short time. Crowds come to Amritsar. The community is growing, organized, confident, and people are noticing.
The week that began in longing for Lahore ends there.

teach.b: Why was the Guru arrested? The sources give more than one answer, and historians weigh them differently.

Jahangir left a memoir, and in it he writes about the Guru with open irritation: too many people, Hindus and Muslims both, were following him, and the emperor wanted it stopped. There was politics too.
Jahangir's son, Prince Khusrau, had rebelled, and the memoir itself says the prince stopped to see the Guru on his way; the Sikh accounts say the Guru blessed him, as he blessed anyone who came.
And Sikh tradition adds a court official, Chandu Shah, with a personal grudge. What the Sikh accounts agree on is what came next.

teach.h: HELD IN THE HEAT OF LAHORE.
teach.b: The Guru was held in Lahore, and in the summer heat he was tortured. Tradition remembers it in terrible detail: made to sit on a red-hot iron plate, with burning sand poured over him. I won't linger there.
What Sikhs linger on is how he sat.
A friend came: Mian Mir, a Muslim Sufi saint of Lahore, whom tradition remembers as close to the Guru. Horrified, he offered to go to the emperor and plead.
Tradition says the Guru calmly told him not to: this too was within God's will, and he would bear it. In the Sikh accounts he did not shout, and did not curse the emperor.
He sat, stayed steady, and kept remembering.
Simran, the word from day fourteen, is doing its hardest work here. Tomorrow, how it ended, and what Sikhs call him because of it.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Arjan's imprisonment and torture in Lahore in the hymns, sermons and stories of his martyrdom anniversary each summer, and the site in Lahore is marked by Gurdwara Dera Sahib.

o: remembering God's name, again and again
a vow of silence kept under pressure
a fast kept in times of trouble

a Muslim Sufi saint tried to help the Guru

the Sikh accounts remember him calm, accepting God's will, and remembering.

games.q: you're Guru Arjan, held in the heat of Lahore. your friend Mian Mir offers to go to the emperor and plead for you. what do you say?
o: no: this too is within God's will.
tell him to raise men and break you out.
games.why: tradition says the Guru calmly declined, saying he would bear what came as God's will. Sikhs remember his steadiness more than his suffering.

practice: Sit still for one minute, then a little longer: hands in your lap, feet on the floor, nothing to fix and nothing to answer. When something wants you to move, an itch, a thought, a sound, don't fight it and don't follow it; stay.
If you remember a name for God, let it ride on your breath; if not, let the breath be your anchor.

wordCard.voice: Simran. Remembering God's name, the practice Guru Arjan kept while tortured in the summer heat at Lahore, staying steady and unshouting.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Lahore, the great city of Punjab where Guru Arjan was held.

carryVoice: Your line: steady in the heat. Thank you for sitting with a hard story. Day sixty-three, and another week behind you.
